{{short description|Mathematical group formed from the automorphisms of an object}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''automorphism group''' of an object ''X'' is the [[group (mathematics)|group]] consisting of [[automorphism]]s of ''X'' under [[Function composition|composition]] of [[morphism]]s.  For example, if ''X'' is a [[Dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] [[vector space]], then the automorphism group of ''X'' is the group of invertible [[linear transformations]] from ''X'' to itself (the [[general linear group]] of ''X'').  If instead ''X'' is a group, then its automorphism group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(X)</math> is the group consisting of all [[group automorphism]]s of ''X''. 

Especially in geometric contexts, an automorphism group is also called a [[symmetry group]]. A subgroup of an automorphism group is sometimes called a '''transformation group'''.

Automorphism groups are studied in a general way in the field of [[category theory]].

== Examples ==
If ''X'' is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] with no additional structure, then any bijection from ''X'' to itself is an automorphism, and hence the automorphism group of ''X'' in this case is precisely the [[symmetric group]] of ''X''.  If the set ''X'' has additional structure, then it may be the case that not all bijections on the set preserve this structure, in which case the automorphism group will be a subgroup of the symmetric group on ''X''.  Some examples of this include the following:
*The automorphism group of a [[field extension]] <math>L/K</math> is the group consisting of field automorphisms of ''L'' that [[fixed-point subring|fix]] ''K''. If the field extension is [[Galois extension|Galois]], the automorphism group is called the [[Galois group]] of the field extension.
*The automorphism group of the [[projective space|projective ''n''-space]] over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] ''k'' is the [[projective linear group]] <math>\operatorname{PGL}_n(k).</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Ch. II, Example 7.1.1.}}</ref>
*The automorphism group <math>G</math> of a finite [[cyclic group]] of [[Order (group theory)|order]] ''n'' is [[Group isomorphism|isomorphic]] to <math>(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times</math>, the [[Multiplicative group of integers modulo n|multiplicative group of integers modulo ''n'']], with the isomorphism given by <math>\overline{a} \mapsto \sigma_a \in G, \, \sigma_a(x) = x^a</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Dummit|Foote|2004|loc=§ 2.3. Exercise 26.}}</ref> In particular, <math>G</math> is an [[abelian group]].
*The automorphism group of a finite-dimensional real [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> has the structure of a (real) [[Lie group]] (in fact, it is even a [[linear algebraic group]]: see [[#Automorphism group functor|below]]). If ''G'' is a Lie group with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, then the automorphism group of ''G'' has a structure of a Lie group induced from that on the automorphism group of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |jstor = 1990752|title = The Automorphism Group of a Lie Group|journal = Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|volume = 72|issue = 2|pages = 209–216|last1 = Hochschild|first1 = G.|year = 1952| doi=10.2307/1990752 }}</ref>{{sfn|Fulton|Harris|1991|loc=Exercise 8.28}}{{efn|First, if ''G'' is simply connected, the automorphism group of ''G'' is that of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. Second, every connected Lie group is of the form <math>\widetilde{G}/C</math> where <math>\widetilde{G}</math> is a simply connected Lie group and ''C'' is a central subgroup and the automorphism group of ''G'' is the automorphism group of <math>G</math> that preserves ''C''. Third, by convention, a Lie group is second countable and has at most coutably many connected components; thus, the general case reduces to the connected case.}}

If ''G'' is a group [[group action|acting]] on a set ''X'', the action amounts to a [[group homomorphism]] from ''G'' to the automorphism group of ''X'' and conversely.  Indeed, each left ''G''-action on a set ''X'' determines <math>G \to \operatorname{Aut}(X), \, g \mapsto \sigma_g, \, \sigma_g(x) = g \cdot x</math>, and, conversely, each homomorphism <math>\varphi: G \to \operatorname{Aut}(X)</math> defines an action by <math>g \cdot x = \varphi(g)x</math>.  This extends to the case when the set ''X'' has more structure than just a set.  For example, if ''X'' is a vector space, then a group action of ''G'' on ''X'' is a ''[[group representation]]'' of the group ''G'', representing ''G'' as a group of linear transformations (automorphisms) of ''X''; these representations are the main object of study in the field of [[representation theory]].

Here are some other facts about automorphism groups:
*Let <math>A, B</math> be two finite sets of the same [[cardinality]] and <math>\operatorname{Iso}(A, B)</math> the set of all [[bijection]]s <math>A \mathrel{\overset{\sim}\to} B</math>. Then <math>\operatorname{Aut}(B)</math>, which is a symmetric group (see above), acts on <math>\operatorname{Iso}(A, B)</math> from the left [[Group_action_(mathematics)#Remarkable properties of actions|freely]] and [[Group_action_(mathematics)#Remarkable properties of actions|transitively]]; that is to say, <math>\operatorname{Iso}(A, B)</math> is a [[torsor]] for <math>\operatorname{Aut}(B)</math> (cf. [[#In category theory]]).
*Let ''P'' be a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]] [[projective module]] over a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R''. Then there is an [[embedding]] <math>\operatorname{Aut}(P) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{GL}_n(R)</math>, unique up to [[inner automorphism]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Milnor|1971|loc=Lemma 3.2.}}</ref>

== In category theory ==
Automorphism groups appear very naturally in [[category theory]].

If ''X'' is an [[Object (category theory)|object]] in a category, then the automorphism group of ''X'' is the group consisting of all the invertible [[morphism]]s from ''X'' to itself. It is the [[unit group]] of the [[endomorphism monoid]] of ''X''. (For some examples, see [[PROP (category theory)|PROP]].)

If <math>A, B</math> are objects in some category, then the set <math>\operatorname{Iso}(A, B)</math> of all <math>A \mathrel{\overset{\sim}\to} B</math> is a left <math>\operatorname{Aut}(B)</math>-[[principal homogeneous space|torsor]]. In practical terms, this says that a different choice of a base point of <math>\operatorname{Iso}(A, B)</math> differs unambiguously by an element of <math>\operatorname{Aut}(B)</math>, or that each choice of a base point is precisely a choice of a trivialization of the torsor.

If <math>X_1</math> and <math>X_2</math> are objects in categories <math>C_1</math> and <math>C_2</math>, and if <math>F: C_1 \to C_2</math> is a [[functor]] mapping <math>X_1</math> to <math>X_2</math>, then <math>F</math> induces a group homomorphism <math>\operatorname{Aut}(X_1) \to \operatorname{Aut}(X_2)</math>, as it maps invertible morphisms to invertible morphisms.

In particular, if ''G'' is a group viewed as a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] with a single object * or, more generally, if ''G'' is a [[groupoid]], then each functor <math>F: G \to C</math>, ''C'' a category, is called an action or a representation of ''G'' on the object <math>F(*)</math>, or the objects <math>F(\operatorname{Obj}(G))</math>. Those objects are then said to be <math>G</math>-objects (as they are acted by <math>G</math>); cf. [[S-object|<math>\mathbb{S}</math>-object]]. If <math>C</math> is a module category like the category of finite-dimensional vector spaces, then <math>G</math>-objects are also called <math>G</math>-modules.

== Automorphism group functor ==
Let <math>M</math> be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field ''k'' that is equipped with some algebraic structure (that is, ''M'' is a finite-dimensional [[algebra over a field|algebra]] over ''k''). It can be, for example, an [[associative algebra]] or a [[Lie algebra]].

Now, consider ''k''-[[linear map]]s <math>M \to M</math> that preserve the algebraic structure: they form a [[vector subspace]] <math>\operatorname{End}_{\text{alg}}(M)</math> of <math>\operatorname{End}(M)</math>. The unit group of <math>\operatorname{End}_{\text{alg}}(M)</math> is the automorphism group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(M)</math>. When a basis on ''M'' is chosen, <math>\operatorname{End}(M)</math> is the space of [[Square matrix|square matrices]] and <math>\operatorname{End}_{\text{alg}}(M)</math> is the zero set of some [[Polynomial|polynomial equations]], and the invertibility is again described by polynomials. Hence, <math>\operatorname{Aut}(M)</math> is a [[linear algebraic group]] over ''k''.

Now base extensions applied to the above discussion determines a functor:<ref>{{harvnb|Waterhouse|2012|loc=§ 7.6.}}</ref> namely, for each [[commutative ring]] ''R'' over ''k'', consider the ''R''-linear maps <math>M \otimes R \to M \otimes R</math> preserving the algebraic structure: denote it by <math>\operatorname{End}_{\text{alg}}(M \otimes R)</math>. Then the unit group of the matrix ring <math>\operatorname{End}_{\text{alg}}(M \otimes R)</math> over ''R'' is the automorphism group <math>\operatorname{Aut}(M \otimes R)</math> and <math>R \mapsto \operatorname{Aut}(M \otimes R)</math> is a [[group functor]]: a functor from the [[Category_of_rings#Category_of_commutative_rings|category of commutative rings]] over ''k'' to the [[category of groups]]. Even better, it is represented by a scheme (since the automorphism groups are defined by polynomials): this scheme is called the '''automorphism group scheme''' and is denoted by <math>\operatorname{Aut}(M)</math>.

In general, however, an automorphism group functor may not be represented by a scheme.
